p.title: A matching theory perspective on legislative organization: assignment of committees

ext.title: Matching theory and Senate committee assignment
ext.venue: Political Science Research and Methods, 1-25 (Original Article; open access)
ext.document_type: Journal article (original research article; formal theory with descriptive and structural empirics)
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 1,916 lines of the extracted file (main text pp. 1-20, references pp. 21-22, appendix Tables A1-A8 and Figure A1 pp. 23-25). Metadata hint confirmed (title, author, 2025, venue, DOI all match the text). Paul's markup: none (no markup files were supplied, so paul_markup is empty). Some appendix tables (A6, A7, A8, Table 1 layout) are garbled in the text extraction; numbers cited below are only those readable without ambiguity.
ext.research_question: How do the US Senate parties actually assign members to committees, i.e., what matching mechanism does each party use to turn rank-ordered committee requests into assignments, and what do those mechanisms imply for strategic reporting, party discipline by the committee-on-committees (COC), incumbents' property rights, and the validity of canonical theories of legislative organization (Distributive, Informational, Cartel-Agenda)? (Sec. 1, pp. 2-3.)
ext.theory: Matching theory (school-choice and house-allocation mechanisms: Serial Dictatorship, Boston mechanism, Top Trading Cycles / YRMH-IGYT, with existing-tenant and property-rights norms). Argues Senate Republicans use a strategyproof seniority-based Serial Dictatorship (equivalent to TTC/YRMH-IGYT in practice) and Senate Democrats use an approximation of the non-strategyproof Boston mechanism with COC tie-breaking. Revisits Distributive (Shepsle-Weingast), Informational (Gilligan-Krehbiel, Krehbiel) and Cartel-Agenda (Cox-McCubbins) theories (Sec. 2 and 4, pp. 3-5 and 16-18). Motivational theories (Mayhew reelection, Fenno power and policy, Ferejohn pork and monetary gain) are background (Sec. 2, p. 4).
ext.data: Three sources. (1) Frisch and Kelly (2006) Senate Democrat committee request data, 80th-103rd Congresses (1947-1995); unit is a Democratic senator's ranked request. (2) Stewart and Woon (2005) Senate committee assignments, 103rd-114th Congresses (1993-2017); unit is a senator-committee assignment. (3) Novel archival dataset of Senate Republican committee requests from the Robert and Elizabeth Dole Archive (University of Kansas) for the 91st and 103rd Congresses (approx. 1969-1971 and 1993-1995); the paper does not report the number of Republican request records. Table A5 uses 104th-114th assignments with per-committee Ns (e.g., Small Business R=31, D=18; Environment R=30, D=14; Rules R=18, D=15). The structural section (Sec. 5.3) uses 426 new Senate committee assignments across 11 sessions (104th-114th), 25 committees and 97 distinct senators; each committee has 7-36 new assignments (fn. 22, p. 20). Ns for Figure 1 and Figure A1 are not reported. Figure A1 notes 76% of Republican non-freshmen rank only one choice, so only first choices are compared.
ext.method: Primarily theoretical and descriptive. (a) Institutional reconstruction of the two procedures from CRS reports (Schneider 2003, 2006, 2014) and Shepsle (1978), with archival correspondence exhibits (Tables 1-2). (b) Mechanism-design analysis: static properties of SD, SD with squatting rights, SD with waiting list, TTC/YRMH-IGYT, and the Boston mechanism (Table 3, citing Abdulkadiroglu-Sonmez 1999, 2003; Kojima-Unver 2014). (c) A two-committee partial-equilibrium model of a single Democrat's rank-order choice against a stochastic environment with an existing-tenant guarantee u(x)>0, yielding Proposition 1 (higher guaranteed payoff implies weakly higher rank positions, p. 15; proof in Online Appendix A.2). (d) Descriptive comparisons: share of rank-1 requests by committee type, freshman vs non-freshman Democrats (Figure 1, p-values); Republican freshman vs non-freshman (Figure A1); average chamber seniority at request (Table A4); cross-party difference in means of seniority at appointment with t-stats and difference in SDs (Table A5); revealed-preference ranking of committee value using average seniority with the 1-3 most senior members excluded (Table A6). (e) Reduced-form structural model u_ic = delta_c + eps_i with eps_i mean 0 and variance sigma_eps^2, identifying committee common value and idiosyncratic variance from the mean and variance of chamber seniority at appointment (and minimum-seniority moments mu_min, sigma_min) for Republicans only (Tables A7-A8), justified by the seniority-based TTC/YRMH-IGYT mechanism. Cross-party comparisons assume the true preference distributions of Republicans and Democrats are the same (p. 19).
ext.identification: No causal identification strategy. The paper calls its evidence "suggestive" (Sec. 5.1, p. 18). Identification of strategic behavior rests on mechanism-design logic: Republicans' SD/TTC mechanism is strategyproof, so reported requests are treated as true preferences (revealed preference), while Democrats' Boston mechanism is not, so requests are treated as strategic and predicted to vary by incumbency. Freshman vs non-freshman contrasts are the within-party comparison (Prediction 3a). Cross-party contrasts of seniority at appointment (Predictions 2b, 2c) are used to infer non-seniority tie-breaking or party discipline by the Democratic COC, under the stated assumption of equal true-preference distributions. Structural estimates of delta_c and sigma_eps are identified only if seniority at appointment reflects the TTC/YRMH-IGYT allocation and the additive utility form holds. Prediction 4 (committee value from seniority, excluding high-seniority members to net out queuing benefits) is argued by revealed preference.
ext.scope: Population: US Senate party committee assignments (Republican and Democratic caucuses). Institution: Senate standing committees, categorized as Constituency, Policy, Prestige and Admin committees (Table A3) and as A/B/C committees (Table A1). Era: Democrat requests 1947-1995; Republican archival requests 91st and 103rd Congresses; assignments 1993-2017 (103rd-114th), with the structural analysis on 104th-114th. Excludes the House as a test case (discussed as background), and post-election seat-ratio negotiations (fn. 9).

key_findings.finding: Senate Republicans assign committees via a seniority-based Serial Dictatorship approximated in practice by the TTC/YRMH-IGYT mechanism; it is strategyproof, individually rational and Pareto efficient. Senate Democrats use an approximation of the Boston mechanism with COC tie-breaking votes, which is not strategyproof. The two parties therefore use structurally different mechanisms.
key_findings.location: Abstract p. 1; Introduction pp. 2-3; Sec. 3.1-3.3 pp. 7-9; Table 3 p. 14; Sec. 3.5.1 pp. 12-14
key_findings.numbers: Table 3: Democrat Boston mechanism is not strategyproof; Republican SD with seniority is strategyproof but not IR; SD with squatting rights is strategyproof but neither IR nor PE; SD with waiting list is strategyproof and IR but not PE; TTC/YRMH-IGYT is strategyproof, IR and PE.

key_findings.finding: Prediction 1 (Republicans request truthfully, Democrats strategically) is supported only by archival anecdote and a CRS quote; the paper says it lacks enough data to test Prediction 1 directly.
key_findings.location: Sec. 3.3 pp. 8-9 (Exhibit #4, Gregg letter 1992); Sec. 5.1 p. 18
key_findings.numbers: No test statistic. Paper states it cannot test Predictions 1, 2(a) and 3(b) (p. 18).

key_findings.finding: Freshman Senate Democrats request fewer popular, highly sought-after Prestige committees than non-freshmen, consistent with hedging against the Boston mechanism when they lack an existing-assignment guarantee.
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.2.1 p. 19; Figure 1 p. 18; Table A4 p. 23
key_findings.numbers: 8% fewer Prestige first-choice requests for freshmen vs non-freshmen, p = 0.15 (Frisch-Kelly 1947-1995 data). Average chamber seniority at request: Prestige 3.88 yrs, Policy 2.89 yrs, Constituency 2.58 yrs.

key_findings.finding: No comparable substitution away from Prestige committees appears among Republican freshmen vs non-freshmen, consistent with strategyproofness of the Republican mechanism.
key_findings.numbers: p = 0.80 for the difference (Dole Archives, 91st and 103rd Congresses). First-choice comparison only, because 76% of Republican non-freshmen rank only one choice.

key_findings.finding: Cross-party differences in seniority at appointment (Predictions 2b, 2c) point to possible party discipline or non-seniority tie-breaking by the Democratic COC on certain committees, not on Prestige and Constituency committees as a group. Environment, Commerce and Governmental Affairs are the flagged policy committees; the text also flags Budget and Rules.
key_findings.numbers: Environment & Public Works: R mean 3.80 (N=30) vs D 1.00 (N=14), diff 2.80, t=3.05, SD diff 5.03. Commerce, Science & Transport: diff -1.74, t=-2.09, SD diff -2.87. Governmental Affairs: diff 4.93, t=1.76, SD diff 1.59. Budget and Rules are called significant in the text under Prediction 2(c), with SD diffs of -6.43 and -4.05 (mean diffs -0.33 and -1.62); the table shows no starred t-stats for these rows.

key_findings.finding: Revealed-preference ranking of committee value (Prediction 4): Rules, Finance, Governmental Affairs and Appropriations are the most sought-after committees, even after excluding the most senior members.
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.2.3 p. 19; Table A6 p. 24 (extraction partly garbled)
key_findings.numbers: Table A6 reports Republican average chamber seniority by committee for all members and excluding the 1, 2 and 3 most senior. Rules is highest in the all-members column at about 16.6 years on the readable entries; per-committee cell mapping is not recoverable from the extraction.

key_findings.finding: Structural reduced-form model (Republicans only): committee common value and idiosyncratic variance can be recovered from the mean and variance of seniority at appointment. Powerful Policy and Prestige committees (Finance, Appropriations) have large common values and small idiosyncratic differences; Constituency committees (Small Business, Armed Services) depend on constituency particulars and have lower common value; Policy committees (Environment, Labor) have large idiosyncratic components.
key_findings.numbers: Sample: 426 new Senate assignments, 25 committees, 97 senators, 104th-114th (fn. 22). Table A7/A8 numeric cells are garbled in extraction, so no mu or sigma values are reported here.

key_findings.finding: Incumbents with a guaranteed existing assignment are more truthful in reporting rank-orders: a Boston-mechanism player with a better guaranteed payoff weakly raises rank positions for each committee (Proposition 1). This gives Prediction 3(b), which the paper says it cannot test with its data.
key_findings.location: Sec. 3.5.2 pp. 14-16; Proposition 1 p. 16; Prediction 3 p. 16; untested per p. 18
key_findings.numbers: Proposition 1: if u(y) > u(x) with y > x, optimal rank-orders satisfy y_i >= x_i for all i. No empirical test reported.

key_findings.finding: Assignment stickiness may reflect mechanism design rather than only specialization: under the Republican mechanism, existing tenants at risk of swaps, and queuing benefits from within-committee seniority, confound the interpretation of high seniority on a committee as revealed value.
key_findings.location: Sec. 3.5.3 pp. 16-17; Prediction 4 p. 16; Figure C1 (online appendix)
key_findings.numbers: None; qualitative argument with the queuing confound acknowledged.

key_findings.finding: Canonical theories: the Distributive Theory anticipates the Democratic mechanism is non-strategyproof but treats equilibrium too naively and does not fit the Republican mechanism. The Informational Theory can explain possible Democratic COC tie-breaking criteria but has difficulty with the Republican mechanism. The Cartel-Agenda channel is largely unavailable to Republican leaders but available to Democratic COC tie-breakers, and only under excess demand.
key_findings.location: Sec. 4 pp. 16-18; Sec. 6 p. 20; three-politician example p. 11
key_findings.numbers: Three-politician, three-committee example: commitment to a tie-breaking rule can produce any of six matchings in the perfectly correlated case; discipline requires excess demand.

key_findings.finding: Worked Republican example: SD gives a non-individually-rational matching (Inc3 loses seat C); SD with squatting rights and SD with waiting list each fail one property; TTC/YRMH-IGYT gives an IR and Pareto-efficient matching.
key_findings.numbers: Example 1 (five seats, four incumbents, one freshman): SD gives (Inc1-D, Inc2-C, Inc3-B, Inc4-E, Fr1-A); TTC/YRMH-IGYT gives (Inc1-D, Inc2-B, Inc3-C, Inc4-E, Fr1-A).

limitations: The paper says its empirical evidence is suggestive only (Sec. 5.1, p. 18), not causal.

No systematic Senate Republican request dataset exists for testing Prediction 1, 2(a) or 3(b) (p. 18). Republican request data are archival, limited to the 91st and 103rd Congresses, and the number of records is not reported.
Cross-party comparisons assume the distribution of true preferences is identical for Republicans and Democrats (p. 19); relaxing this would need matching or structural estimation, which was not done.
Only first-choice requests are compared for Republicans, because 76% of non-freshman Republicans rank one choice (Figure A1 note, p. 25).
The freshman vs non-freshman Democratic difference (8%, p = 0.15) is not significant at conventional levels.
The Democratic Boston mechanism is approximated; COC tie-breaking votes are secret and unobserved, so a Democratic structural model cannot be estimated (fn. 21, p. 20).
The structural model is reduced form; richer models with politician- and session-specific terms could not be estimated (fn. 22, p. 20), with 426 assignments across 97 senators.
Republican strategyproofness is supported partly by archival anecdote (Exhibit #4) and the Dole letter (Exhibit #5); Exhibit #6 (sequential implementation) is also anecdotal.
Interdependent preferences (over who else sits on a committee, or House counterparts) would break strategyproofness of both mechanisms (fn. 13, p. 9).
The author treats seniority-only tie-breaking as unlikely for Democrats (p. 18), but rival tie-breaking criteria are not formally tested.
Queuing benefits and specialization stickiness confound interpreting high seniority on a committee as revealed value (p. 16).
Party discipline is modeled only through Democratic COC tie-breaking; Republican leader influence is shown only through the Dole exhibits (Sec. 3.4, pp. 10-11).
The Republican mechanism is a static SD/TTC approximation; dynamic rules and sequential implementation are simplified (fn. 7 p. 6; fn. 17 p. 14).
Excludes the House, post-election seat-ratio negotiations (fn. 9, p. 7), and does not model policy effects of committee membership.
measures: Committee categories: Constituency, Policy, Prestige, Admin (Table A3); A/B/C administrative categories (Table A1).
Rank-1 request share by committee type, freshman vs non-freshman (Figure 1, Figure A1).
Chamber seniority (years) at request (Table A4) and at appointment (Table A5): means, SDs, Ns, t-statistics, cross-party differences in means and SDs.
Average chamber seniority of committee members, all members and excluding the 1, 2 and 3 most senior (Table A6), as a revealed-preference value measure.

Structural: committee common value delta_c and idiosyncratic variance sigma_eps^2 from mean and variance of chamber seniority at appointment (mu, sigma), and minimum seniority at appointment (mu_min, sigma_min) (Tables A7-A8).
Existing-tenant status (freshman vs incumbent) and guaranteed payoff from existing assignment (Proposition 1).
Within-committee seniority ranks (chair and ranking-member exclusion) for the queuing-benefit control (Prediction 4).

short_quotes.quote: Republicans and Democrats use two distinct matching mechanisms, such that canonical theories of parties cannot apply equally to them.
The Republican mechanism is strategyproof, whereas the Democrat mechanism incentivizes politicians to manipulate their reported preferences.
freshmen Senate Democrats request 8% fewer popular, highly sought-after Prestige committees compared to non-freshmen

rel.summary_md:
Thakur (PSRM 2025) applies matching theory to US Senate committee assignment. He argues that the two parties fill seats through different mechanisms. Senate Republicans use a seniority-ordered Serial Dictatorship, which works in practice like the strategyproof, individually rational and Pareto-efficient TTC/YRMH-IGYT. Senate Democrats use something close to the Boston mechanism, with secret tie-breaking votes by the committee-on-committees (COC). Under the Boston mechanism, members have reason to misreport their preferences.

The evidence is explicitly suggestive.
- Freshman Democrats list Prestige committees as first choice 8% less often than non-freshmen (p = 0.15, 1947-1995 request data). Republicans show no such gap (p = 0.80).
- Mean seniority at appointment differs across parties on some committees (e.g., Environment & Public Works: R 3.80, N=30, vs D 1.00, N=14; t=3.05). The author reads this as possible COC discipline on the Democratic side.
- A reduced-form structural model for Republicans only (426 new assignments, 104th-114th) finds high common value and small idiosyncratic variance for Finance and Appropriations. Constituency committees such as Small Business have low common value and depend on constituency particulars.
- Seniority on a committee mixes revealed value with queuing benefits.

For Paul's system, the paper speaks mainly to the committee/Influence pillar. That pillar prices seats by CU-relevance tier, with fixed chair and ranking multipliers. It does not distinguish chamber or party. The paper suggests that who holds a seat is partly an artifact of party-specific mechanisms, seniority queues and COC discipline. This bears on Paul's chicken-or-egg note about partisanship and committee selection. It also argues against treating committee office as a costly, member-chosen signal, which agrees with the system dropping committee gatekeeping (path J) from the say-do gate.

Scope limits: Senate only (about 100 of 533 members), data from 1947-2017, the House not studied, and no causal identification. None of this validates the tier weights. Any test of the committee pillar against outcomes should be stratified by party and chamber, or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Senate seat allocation runs through two different party mechanisms. Republicans use seniority-ordered SD/TTC (strategyproof). Democrats use a Boston approximation with secret COC tie-breaking. Cross-party seniority-at-appointment gaps on some committees point to party discipline: Environment & Public Works R 3.80 (N=30) vs D 1.00 (N=14), diff 2.80, t=3.05; Commerce diff -1.74, t=-2.09; 104th-114th assignments. So who holds a given seat reflects mechanism, seniority queue and party selection, not only member choice or structural power.
bearings.system_side: Influence% = committee_raw/MAX, built from seat tokens priced by CU-relevance tier (Highly 3.0 / Moderately 1.8 / Slightly 0.9; subcommittee 1/6) with chair, ranking and vice multipliers. The same rule applies to every member regardless of chamber or party, and the result is weighted at 40% of the composite. The pillar treats a held seat as structural CU power.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Covers only the Senate rows (about 100 of 533). The paper does not study the House or the 119th-Congress rules, and its evidence is suggestive (p. 18). The bearing does not challenge the CU-relevance tiers, which are owner policy. It says that any test of whether committee score predicts CU outcomes should be stratified by party and chamber, or labelled UNSTRATIFIED, because selection into seats differs by party. Moderate at most, since the cross-party gaps are significant on only a few committees.

bearings.paper_claim: Committees differ in common value. In the Republican structural model, Finance and Appropriations have large common value and small idiosyncratic variance. Constituency committees such as Small Business (R N=31, D N=18) have lower common value and are sought for constituency-specific reasons. Rules, Finance, Governmental Affairs and Appropriations are the most sought after even after excluding the 1-3 most senior members. High within-committee seniority mixes value with queuing benefits.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.2.3 and 5.3 pp. 19-20; Prediction 4 p. 16; Tables A6-A8 pp. 24-25; Sec. 3.5.3 pp. 16-17
bearings.system_side: Every Small Business seat token reads [Highly] (74 of 74 on the live sheet, per the module docstring). Chair and ranking multipliers are fixed constants (Chair full 3.0 / sub 7.5). Seat weight encodes CU relevance only, with no term for prestige or for how competitive the seat is to obtain.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Matters only if the pillar is meant to measure power as well as CU relevance. A seat on a low-common-value constituency committee may signal constituency interest, which could be an alignment cue, rather than leverage. Senate Republicans 1995-2017 only; Table A7/A8 cell values are garbled in extraction. Do not use this to re-tier; it is a validity caveat.

bearings.paper_claim: Committee placement is produced by party mechanisms: seniority order for Republicans, and Boston-style allocation plus COC tie-breaking for Democrats. Reported requests are strategic for Democrats, and freshmen hedge away from Prestige committees (8% fewer first choices, p=0.15). A seat is therefore not a clean, member-chosen, costly revealed action.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p. 1; Sec. 3.3 pp. 8-9; Sec. 5.2.1 p. 19; Proposition 1 p. 16
bearings.system_side: The cell gate corroborates Champion/Defender only through path A (authored or original-cosponsored bill) or path V (CU-aligned final-passage vote). Path J (committee gatekeeping) was removed on the premise that committee office is not an action.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports excluding seat-holding as corroboration. It does not speak to committee actions such as markup votes. Senate evidence only, descriptive, not causal.

gaps_exposed: The committee pillar is the same for both chambers and both parties. Nothing records how the seat was obtained (seniority queue vs COC selection) or the member's seniority. The paper shows that selection into seats differs by party, so committee-score validity is untested within strata.

There is no committee-value (prestige or common-value) term separate from CU relevance. A Highly seat on a low-common-value constituency committee such as Small Business and a Highly seat on a high-value policy committee are priced identically.
Chair and ranking multipliers ignore that Senate leadership largely follows within-committee seniority queues. The paper flags queuing benefits as confounding seniority read as value.
flags: The pillar effectively pools across a fault line the paper identifies: the Republican seniority mechanism vs Democratic COC tie-breaking. Any committee-score coefficient or correlation against outcomes must be reported by party (and chamber), or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.

The paper's evidence is self-described as suggestive. Key contrasts are not significant at conventional levels (Democrat freshman gap p=0.15), and Table A6-A8 numbers are garbled in extraction. Do not quote committee value estimates from it.
Senate only (about 100 of 533 members). Nothing transfers to House seat-holders without separate evidence.
This mapping is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Hall & Wayman (1990) and Fouirnaies & Hall (2018), cited here on lobbying and committee access, are background only. Neither licenses access or influence language for committee seats in the system.
rel.paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's committee-pillar note flagging a chicken-or-egg problem between partisanship and committee selection. It gives a mechanism for that worry: Democratic COC tie-breaking can discipline placement, while Republican placement is mostly seniority. The paper does not support Paul's broader premise that committees are the structural power layer (Porter) in any way that would underwrite the tier weights or the 40% Influence weight. Those weights remain owner policy that this paper does not test. Paul's note is not stale; the system has since removed committee gatekeeping from the say-do gate, which fits this paper. The note does not yet record that seat selection differs by party, which matters for any future validation of the committee pillar.

related.why: Porter maps House committee structure as networks of shared membership. Thakur explains how Senate seats are allocated, which bears on whether shared-membership ties reflect choice or party mechanism.
A House committee-request codebook is the same kind of request data as Thakur's Frisch-Kelly and Dole archive requests. It could support a House version of his freshman vs incumbent request tests.

Paul cites Huneeus & Kim's committee-assignment instrument. Thakur's finding that placement follows party-specific mechanisms (seniority vs COC discipline) bears on how exogenous assignment is as an instrument.
Paul reads Gaynor as showing that party leadership shapes members' insulation. Thakur models leader and COC discipline over committee placement, a parallel party-control channel.
